title: Apologeticus Contra Recentes Impugnatorem
author: Flavius Lucius Dexter

passages.original: quem anno Christi 390 ela- boratum ex fine illius manifestum est, et probat Baron, in Annal. Eccles. 2° Quod dicat opus suum ad manus Hieronymi ut pote jam defuncti perve- nire nequivisse; quis autem credat ab anno Domini 390 quo, teste Hieronymo, liber scriptus erat, usque ad 426 quo, vel ipso Dextro concedente, Hieronymus in humanis esse desiit 36 annorum intercapedine, opus sibi a potentissimo viro dica- tum, numquam accepisse? 3°quod in eadem epi- stola fateatur auctor illius, cum illud opus Orosio nuncupavit, viguisse annum Christi 430 et in fine suae historiae Dexter scribit, quando illam absolvit floruisse annum 440.
passages.english: that it was composed in the year of Christ 390 is evident from its end, and Baronius proves it in the Ecclesiastical Annals. 2nd, that he says his work could not reach the hands of Jerome, since he was already dead; but who would believe that from the year of the Lord 390, in which, on Jerome's testimony, the book had been written, up to 426, in which, even by Dexter's own admission, Jerome ceased to be among the living, over an interval of 36 years, he never received a work dedicated to him by a most powerful man? 3rd, that in the same letter its author admits that when he dedicated that work to Orosius he was alive in the year of Christ 430, and at the end of his history Dexter writes that when he finished it he was flourishing in the year 440.

passages.original: Sub ann. 400, mittitur Orosius legatus Hispa- norum antistitum ad Africani cujusdam concilii Pa- tres, presbyter quidem jam ordinatus, ut liquet ex epist. 90 Augustini : et tamen natus dicitur in hoc Chronico anno Domini 384, ex quo sextum decimum annum non excessisse probatur. Quae rerum, quaeso, convenientia?
passages.english: Around the year 400 Orosius was sent as envoy of the Spanish bishops to the Fathers of a certain African council, being already an ordained priest, as is clear from Augustine's letter 90; and yet in this Chronicle he is said to have been born in the year of the Lord 384, from which it is shown that he had not passed his sixteenth year. What consistency, I ask, is there in these things?

passages.original: Primo namque sub anno 432, Isidorum auctorem libri Allegoriarum vocat Seniorem; discordans a Dextro, qui eum vo- cavit Juniorem, ad annum 430, et cum illo dedi- casse asserat Allegoriarum librum Paulo Orosio Tarraconensi, hic Paulo Orosio Legionensi episcopo nuncupatum contendit.
passages.english: For first, under the year 432, he calls Isidore, the author of the Book of Allegories, 'the Elder', disagreeing with Dexter, who called him 'the Younger' at the year 430; and whereas [Dexter] asserts that he dedicated the Book of Allegories to Paulus Orosius of Tarragona, this [writer] maintains that it was dedicated to Paulus Orosius, bishop of León.

passages.original: Anno 373. S. Donatus regulam Eremitarum S. Augustini locupletiorem mitioremque primus ex Africa in Hispani is invexisse dicitur, et Servitanum monasterium construxisse. Stolidum sane commentum (ait censor): Augustini siquidem regula mitior est omnibus, indigetque restrictione, non mitigatione C. Quod Dei timorem de statu monachorum. Et D. Ilde- fonsus ac caeteri rerum Hispanicarum scriptores, cum de S. Donato agunt regulae Augustini non me- minerunt;
passages.english: Year 373. St Donatus is said to have been the first to bring from Africa into Spain the rule of the Hermits of St Augustine, richer and milder, and to have built the Servitan monastery. A stupid fabrication indeed (says the critic): for the rule of Augustine is milder than all, and needs tightening, not mitigation. [...] And St Ildefonsus and the other writers on Spanish affairs, when they treat of St Donatus, make no mention of the rule of Augustine;
passages.notes: 'C. Quod Dei timorem de statu monachorum' appears to be a garbled reference (perhaps a canon-law citation, c. 'Quod Dei timorem', De statu monachorum); left untranslated.

passages.original: Posterioris ti- tulus est, De Sacerdotibus monasterii : ubi de his, qui post monachatum ad ordines evehuntur multa disponit. Certe si Pennottus titulos capitum Regulae dumtaxat legeret, ab eo errore liberaretur. Sed hoc simile est ci, quod de Paulo Orosio scribit lib. I, cap. 38, num. 4, nimirum nomen monachorum tam late apud ipsum acceptum fuisse lib. VII suae Ormestae cap. 17, quod omnes Christianos illos comprehen- deret, qui ad unum fidei opus, dimissa soecularium rerum multimoda actione, se redigebant; quo pacto ait Pennottus etiam clericos regulares sub nomine monachorum comprehendi. Sed si verba ab Orosio immediate subjecta legisset (ut omittam perperam citasse cap.
passages.english: The title of the latter is 'On the Priests of the Monastery', where he lays down many provisions concerning those who are raised to orders after becoming monks. Certainly, if Pennottus had only read the chapter titles of the Rule, he would be freed from that error. But this is like what he writes about Paulus Orosius in book I, chapter 38, number 4, namely that the name of monks was taken so broadly by him in book VII of his Ormesta, chapter 17, that it included all those Christians who, having given up the manifold business of worldly affairs, devoted themselves to the one work of faith; in which way, Pennottus says, regular clerics too are included under the name of monks. But if he had read the words Orosius places immediately after (to pass over that he cited the chapter wrongly

passages.original: Rursus monasterium de Alna (sic enim vocatur, non Alva) solos quatuor annos S. Augustini regulam professum fuerat, ut tradit Miraeus in Chron. Cist. ad ann. Domini 1148 : unde cum in ejus institutis tenerum adhuc esset, facile fuit ad alia praestantiora transire. Ubi autem, quaeso, Pennottus invenit mo- nasterium istud Eboracense ex quo prior cum aliis fratribus ad Cistercienses pervolaverat, fuisse ordinis canonici?
passages.english: Again, the monastery of Alna (for so it is called, not Alva) had professed the rule of St Augustine for only four years, as Miraeus relates in the Cistercian Chronicle at the year of the Lord 1148; hence, since it was still young in its observances, it was easy to pass over to other, more excellent ones. But where, I ask, did Pennottus find that this monastery of York, from which the prior with other brothers had flown over to the Cistercians, was of the canonical order?

passages.original: Quartus ordo institutus est in Africa a B. Augustino; et ipse designatus est in Juda. Quintus ordo fuit canonicorum regularium in occiduis partibus institutus, qui pro parte ipsius reguloe quam tenet di- citur et ipse S. Augustini : et ipse designatus est in Issachar. Sextus ordo videtur esse canonicorum Proe- monstratentium : et ipse designatus est in Zabulon· Hoec de filiis Lioe. His de sex ordinibus clericorum dictis, subinfert de totidem ordinibus monachorum.
passages.english: The fourth order was instituted in Africa by Blessed Augustine; and it is signified in Judah. The fifth order was that of the canons regular instituted in the western parts, which, on account of the rule it holds, is itself also called St Augustine's; and it is signified in Issachar. The sixth order seems to be that of the Premonstratensian canons; and it is signified in Zebulun. So much for the sons of Leah. Having spoken of these six orders of clerics, he goes on to speak of as many orders of monks.

passages.original: Immo ob id potius Higinius ad Leronem relegatus est, quod insula esset serpentibus plena, ut certius moreretur : et idcirco forsan dolebat Ambrosius ad Valentinianum scribens, exsilium senis. Vide quae hac de re diximus ad annum 384.
passages.english: On the contrary, Hyginus was banished to Lero rather for this reason, that the island was full of serpents, so that he might die the more surely; and that is perhaps why Ambrose, writing to Valentinian, lamented the old man's exile. See what we said on this matter at the year 384.

passages.original: Quod de duplici Leporio dicitur, parum constare probavimus in comment. ad an. 406, ubi Pennotto suppresso nomine respondimus, qui tamen inde prae- cipue movetur, ne videlicet reperiretur discipulus aliquis Augustini : ad haeresim declinasse. Sed hoc leve admodum est; nec minuit tanti pastoris gloriam una morbida ovis, sicut nec Christi magisterium unus Judas, eo praesertim quod postmodum Lepo- rius iste opera ipsius Augustini scribitur ad bonam mentem redactus.
passages.english: What is said about a double Leporius we have shown to be poorly established in the commentary at the year 406, where we answered Pennottus without naming him; he is however moved chiefly by this, namely that no disciple of Augustine should be found to have fallen into heresy. But this is a very slight matter; one diseased sheep does not lessen the glory of so great a shepherd, just as one Judas does not lessen Christ's teaching, especially since this Leporius is afterwards recorded to have been brought back to a right mind through the efforts of Augustine himself.

passages.original: Recte quidem ait Maximus Paulum Orosium obiisse centenario majorem anno Christi 471, cum natus fuerit 370, ut correctiores codices habent, de quo in responsione ad 11 objectum adversum Dextrum, satis diximus.
passages.english: Maximus rightly says that Paulus Orosius died at over a hundred years of age in the year of Christ 471, since he was born in 370, as the more correct manuscripts have it; about which we have said enough in the reply to the 11th objection against Dexter.

passages.original: Quid si hac in re dormitavit Maximus? nam de tempore mortis clarissimorum virorum saepissime dubitatum est, ut Augustini, Hieronymi, et aliorum : et aliquando bonus dormitat Homerus : solis quidem sacris auctoribus datum coelitus est, nusquam labi.
passages.english: What if Maximus nodded off on this point? For there has very often been doubt about the time of death of the most illustrious men, such as Augustine, Jerome, and others; and sometimes even good Homer nods. Indeed, it has been granted from heaven to the sacred authors alone never to slip.
passages.notes: "Bonus dormitat Homerus" echoes Horace, Ars Poetica 359. The Maximus meant is not identified in the passage.
